newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat tests young Israeli leader.
newsitem.headline: Arafat tests young Israeli leader.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat won a summit in Washington and drew world attention to the slow pace of Arab-Israeli peace by vigorously challenging the policies of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

A leader of the Palestine Liberation Organisation for nearly three decades, Arafat, 67, tested the mettle of the 46-year-old Netanyahu in four days of clashes in the West Bank, Gaza and Jerusalem last week in which 57 Arabs and 15 Jews died.

The violence was triggered by Israel's opening of an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem, but tensions have been simmering since Netanyahu was elected in May on a platform rejecting the principle of land-for-peace.

A hero for some and a ruthless guerrilla for others, Arafat is instantly recognisable to the world with his stubble of beard and chequered headdress folded carefully in the shape of the Palestinian homeland for which he has fought tirelessly.

Arafat took perhaps his biggest gamble of all when he sealed a PLO-Israel peace accord with a handshake with his old nemesis, the late Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, in Washington on September 13, 1993.

Returning in 1994 to the Gaza Strip -- part of the embryo homeland under the accord -- the one-time symbol of Palestinian unity found himself facing Moslem militants attacking Israel and threatening their peace deal.

Suicide bombings that claimed 59 lives in Israel last February and March drew heavy Israeli pressure to crack down on the Hamas and Islamic Jihad groups. Arafat arrested hundreds of Islamic activists.

But Israel, citing security concerns, kept a closure clamped on the West Bank and Gaza, causing economic hardship and undermining support for Arafat, elected Palestinian president by an overwhelming majority in January.

At first snubbed by Netanyahu, who said he preferred not to meet him, Arafat pushed the prime minister towards their first meeting on September 4 by ordering the first general strike in the West Bank and Gaza in two years in protest at Israeli policies.

Arafat refused to meet Netanyahu one-on-one last week after the violence erupted, leading U.S. President Bill Clinton to invite them, Jordan's King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak -- who declined to come -- to a White House summit.

Arafat kept the PLO alive through unequal battles against Israeli forces and Arab governments anxious to control him. He has survived plots and assassination attempts -- and an air crash -- since becoming PLO chairman in 1969. There is no one of his stature in the PLO to replace him.

"The thing that keeps me going, the most precious thing that is always on my mind, is the regaining of dignity for the Palestinian people, and restoring the name of Palestine to the map of the Middle East," he says.
Short and bald, Arafat hardly cuts a heroic figure. But to Palestinians -- even those lukewarm about his policies -- he is known as Abu Ammar, his nom de guerre, or just as al-Khityar, the old man.

Born in Cairo on August 24, 1929, he took part in battles between Arabs and Jews in the emerging Israel in 1948. He set up a successful engineering business in Kuwait before devoting himself to the cause of gaining a Palestinian homeland in 1965.
He grabbed headlines as spokesman for a new breed of Palestinian -- the young fedayeen, dispossessed, angry and dedicated to armed struggle against the Jewish state.
The defeat of the Arab armies by Israel in the 1967 war led to the Palestinians taking their cause into their own hands.

Arafat toured the globe with all the trappings of a head of state and became a champion to many in the Third World. He remained head of the PLO through its violent ejection from Jordan in 1970 and expulsion from Beirut after the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon.
In the 1980s, he began a new diplomatic tack towards peace and basked in international sympathy generated by the uprising against Israeli rule in the occupied territories.
For years a bachelor who said he was tied to the Palestinian struggle, Arafat married Suha Tawil, a Palestinian Christian researcher half his age in 1992. They had a daughter last year.
